proposals.title: HB0025 With Chemotherapy for Advanced Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer
proposals.abstract: Importance Bispecific antibodies targeting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)/PD-1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) pathways represent a promising therapeutic strategy for advanced non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). HB0025 is a novel bispecific antibody fusion targeting PD-L1 and VEGF. Objective To evaluate the efficacy and safety of HB0025 plus chemotherapy in previously untreated advanced, driver variant–negative NSCLC. Design, Setting, and Participants This open-label, multicenter, phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial enrolled patients with stage IIIB/C or IV NSCLC without sensitizing EGFR, ALK, or ROS1 alterations across 13 hospitals in China. Participants included those with nonsquamous NSCLC and squamous NSCLC. Patients were enrolled from January 15, 2024, to May 21, 2025. Data cutoff was April 20, 2026. Interventions Patients received intravenous 10-mg/kg HB0025 every 3 weeks or 20-mg/kg HB0025 every 3 weeks plus chemotherapy: pemetrexed/carboplatin for nonsquamous and paclitaxel/carboplatin for squamous for up to 6 cycles, followed by HB0025 maintenance (with pemetrexed for nonsquamous) until disease progression or unacceptable toxic effects. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary end points were safety and investigator-assessed objective response rate (ORR) per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, version 1.1. The secondary end points included disease control rate, duration of response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Results Treatment efficacy was evaluable in 169 enrolled patients. The nonsquamous cohort included 85 patients (median [IQR] age, 63.0 [58.0-68.0] years; 26 [30.6%] female and 59 [69.4%] male patients), and the squamous cohort included 84 patients (median [IQR] age, 65.0 [60.0-69.0] years; 6 [7.1%] female and 78 [92.9%] male patients). In the nonsquamous cohort, confirmed ORR was 36.4% (95% CI, 17.2%-59.3%) and 57.1% (95% CI, 44.1%-69.5%) in the 10-mg/kg and 20-mg/kg dose groups, respectively. In the squamous cohort, ORR reached 68.2% (95% CI, 45.1%-86.1%) and 74.2% (95%, 61.5%-84.5%) at the respective doses. Median PFS was 12.52 months (95% CI, 10.15-16.56) in the nonsquamous cohort and 14.78 months (95% CI, 11.30 to not estimable) in the squamous cohort. The 12-month PFS rates were 54.3% (95% CI, 41.6%-65.3%) and 62.1% (95% CI, 49.9%-72.1%) in the nonsquamous and squamous cohorts, and the 12-month OS rates were 75.8% (95% CI, 65.0%-83.7%) and 85.5% (95% CI, 75.8%-91.5%), respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 56 of 85 patients (65.9%) in the nonsquamous cohort and 51 of 84 (60.7%) in the squamous cohort, mainly as hematologic toxic effects. Any-grade immune-related adverse events related to HB0025 occurred in 20 patients (23.5%) in the nonsquamous cohort and 21 patients (25%) in the squamous cohort. Conclusions In this phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial, HB0025 plus chemotherapy showed promising antitumor activity and manageable safety in patients with advanced, driver variant–negative NSCLC in both nonsquamous and squamous histologic types, supporting further evaluation in randomized phase 3 clinical trials. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06758557

proposals.title: Activity and safety of first-line pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel in triple-negative breast cancer: a single-arm, phase 1b/2 trial
proposals.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pumitamig, an investigational bispecific antibody targeting programmed death ligand-1 and vascular endothelial growth factor A, has shown preliminary efficacy across several tumour types. We aimed to evaluate the safety and activity of pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel as first-line treatment in patients with advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. METHODS: In this single-arm, phase 1b/2 trial conducted at ten sites (hospitals and cancer centres) in China, patients aged 18-75 years with histologically documented, unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 or less, and one or more measurable lesion (as per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours, version 1.1) received first-line pumitamig (20 mg/kg intravenously once every 2 weeks) plus nab-paclitaxel (100 mg/m2 intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle) until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. In phase 1b, six patients received pumitamig (20 mg/kg once every 2 weeks intravenously plus nab-paclitaxel 100 mg/m2 intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle) and were monitored for treatment-emergent adverse events, before subsequent enrolment in phase 2. The primary endpoints were confirmed objective response rate and safety, assessed in the efficacy-evaluable population, defined as all patients who received one or more doses of study drug and had measurable disease at baseline and at least one efficacy assessment. This trial is registered with chictr.org.cn (ChiCTR2200060400) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05918133), and is closed to recruitment. FINDINGS: Between June 27, 2022, and March 15, 2023, 42 patients were enrolled, received one or more doses of pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel (median duration of exposure 9·0 months, 95% CI 6·9-11·7) and had one or more tumour assessments. All patients were Chinese and female; median age was 53 years (IQR 41-60). At a median follow-up of 35·2 months (95% CI 33·0-36·1), the confirmed objective response rate was 73·8% (95% CI 58·0-86·1; 31 of 42 patients), including one complete response and 30 partial responses. The most frequent treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or worse were decreased neutrophil count (13 [31%] of 42 patients), decreased white blood cell count (11 [26%]), proteinuria (six [14%]), and febrile neutropenia (five [12%]). Nine (21%) patients reported 14 treatment-related serious adverse events (alanine aminotransferase increased n=2; febrile neutropenia n=2; pancreatitis n=2; and ascites, aspartate aminotransferase increased, abdominal distension, γ-glutamyltransferase increased, blood alkaline phosphatase increased, cataract, macular oedema, and retinal vein occlusion all n=1). Treatment-related adverse events led to discontinuation of both nab-paclitaxel and pumitamig in four (10%) patients, discontinuation of nab-paclitaxel only in three (7%) patients, and discontinuation of pumitamig only in two (5%) patients. There were no treatment-related deaths. INTERPRETATION: Treatment with first-line pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel showed encouraging antitumour activity in patients with advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer and a safety profile consistent with the mode of actions of both agents. These findings warrant further clinical evaluation in global phase 2 and 3 trials. FUNDING: Biotheus (BioNTech group). TRANSLATION: For the Chinese translation of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

proposals.title: Neoadjuvant botensilimab with or without balstilimab in pMMR and dMMR colon cancer: the phase 2 UNICORN trial
proposals.abstract: Preoperative immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are active in patients with deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) colon cancer (CC), whereas proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) CC has been consistently considered resistant to first-generation ICIs. In the phase 2 UNICORN trial, we evaluated short-course preoperative botensilimab (BOT; multifunctional Fc-enhanced anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody) alone or in combination with the anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody balstilimab (BOT + BAL) in 56 patients with resectable, locally advanced CC. Twenty-eight patients with pMMR CC were sequentially enrolled in BOT (n = 14) and BOT + BAL (n = 14) cohorts. Twenty-eight patients with dMMR CC followed the same sequential allocation strategy. The primary endpoint of centrally assessed pathological major response (pMR) rate (≤10% of residual viable tumor) was met in all cohorts, except pMMR BOT. Specifically, the pMR rate was 0% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0-23.2%) in pMMR BOT, 36% (95% CI: 12.8-64.9%) in pMMR BOT + BAL, 36% (95% CI: 12.8-64.9%) in dMMR BOT and 100% (95% CI: 76.8-100%) in dMMR BOT + BAL. Secondary endpoints included safety, quality of life, describing treatment-induced transcriptional dynamics, peripheral blood mononuclear cell dynamics, radiomics and radiogenomics features, fecal microbiota composition and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) dynamics. Eight (29%) and 15 (54%) patients treated with BOT and BOT + BAL, respectively, experienced immune-related adverse events, most commonly flu-like syndrome and diarrhea. Single-cell spatial transcriptomic analysis of matched baseline and post-treatment samples highlighted high baseline PD-L1 stromal expression and low post-treatment regulatory T cell signatures in pMMR responders, whereas dMMR responders displayed high baseline FCGR2A and FCGR3A expression on intratumoral macrophages. Clearance of ctDNA before surgery correlated with pathological response and lack of recurrence at data cutoff. Preoperative BOT + BAL elicits pathological responses in patients with pMMR or dMMR CC, supporting the combination as a promising strategy to expand ICI benefits to the early-stage setting. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05845450 .

proposals.title: Perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy in resectable non-small cell lung cancer: a phase 2 trial
proposals.abstract: Resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) carries a high risk of postoperative recurrence, underscoring the need for effective perioperative therapies. This nonrandomized, noncomparative phase 2 trial evaluated neoadjuvant ivonescimab monotherapy (cohort 1) or in combination with chemotherapy (cohort 2), followed by surgery and adjuvant ivonescimab. In cohort 2, the major pathological response (MPR) rate was 70.1% (47/67; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 57.7-80.7); the lower bound of the 80% two-sided CI exceeded the historical control rate of 41% and the primary endpoint was met. The MPR rate in cohort 1 was 60.0% (6/10; 95% CI = 26.2-87.8). Among patients who achieved MPR, 83.3% (5/6) in cohort 1 and 97.9% (46/47) in cohort 2 had residual viable tumor (RVT) of ≤5%, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 36.4% (4/11) patients in cohort 1 and 30.4% (24/79) of those in cohort 2, with no grade 3 or higher hemorrhage or treatment-related death. Treatment-related surgery delay occurred in one (1.3%) patient. Surgery-related AEs related to ivonescimab occurred in 10.0% (1/10) and 10.4% (7/67) patients in the two cohorts, respectively, with no grade 3 or higher events reported. These data support perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy as a promising strategy for resectable NSCLC. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05247684 .

proposals.title: Regulatable membrane-bound IL-15 engineered TIL cell therapy for immune checkpoint inhibitor-resistant advanced melanoma: pooled analysis of phase 1 and 1/2 trials
proposals.abstract: Amsokigene autoleucel (amsoki-cel, OBX-115) is a tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) cell therapy engineered to express acetazolamide (ACZ)-regulatable membrane-bound interleukin-15, abrogating the need for interleukin-2. In two single-arm trials (completed phase 1 single-center first-in-human (FIH) and ongoing phase 1/2 multicenter Agni-01), patients with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-resistant advanced melanoma received lymphodepletion and varying doses and schedules of amsoki-cel and ACZ. The primary objective of FIH and Agni-01 phase 1 was safety, tolerability and recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D); the primary objective of Agni-01 phase 2 was objective response rate (ORR) at the RP2D. The first patient treated experienced rapid lymphocyte expansion and vasogenic edema of a previously irradiated brain metastasis, prompting protocol modifications and dose deescalation in FIH, including 80% reduction in maximum amsoki-cel dose and 75% reduction in ACZ dose. After preliminary demonstration of safety at the lower dose, doses were increased in FIH, and reescalation was initiated in Agni-01. Across studies, 37 patients were treated (FIH, n = 17; Agni-01, n = 20). Post hoc pooled analysis demonstrated no dose-limiting toxicities, ICU care or treatment-related mortality. Most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) included neutropenia (64.9% (24/37)), leukopenia/lymphopenia (56.8% (21/37) each) and anemia/thrombocytopenia (37.8% (14/37) each). Serious TEAEs were reported for 10 patients, including eight patients with grade 3 or higher events (non-hematologic, 13.5% (5/37); hematologic, 13.5% (5/37)). RP2D was selected based on overall safety and tolerability as well as preliminary anti-tumor activity in Agni-01 phase 1. The phase 2 preliminary ORR was 66.7% (6/9). In total, 15 patients were treated at RP2D and comprise the Key Efficacy Set (Agni-01: phase 1, n = 6; phase 2, n = 9), of which 10 patients (66.7%; 95% confidence interval 38-88%) achieved objective responses (including two complete responses). Amsoki-cel demonstrated favorable safety and promising early clinical activity in patients with ICI-resistant melanoma. A separate phase 2 pivotal Agni-01 cohort is ongoing. ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT05470283 and NCT06060613 .

proposals.title: Evolving First-Line Treatment Strategies in ERBB2 -Positive Metastatic Breast Cancer
proposals.abstract: Importance The treatment landscape of ERBB2 (formerly HER2)–positive metastatic breast cancer has evolved substantially during the past decade, with emerging therapies challenging the long-standing induction-maintenance paradigm established by the CLEOPATRA trial (NCT00567190). However, optimal treatment selection, sequencing, and duration remain uncertain, particularly in the context of increasing therapeutic complexity and biologic heterogeneity. Observations Taxane-based chemotherapy combined with trastuzumab and pertuzumab has long been the standard first-line induction regimen, followed by maintenance anti- ERBB2 therapy with or without endocrine therapy based on hormone receptor status. Recent data from the DESTINY-Breast09 trial (DB09; NCT04784715) demonstrate superior progression-free survival with trastuzumab deruxtecan plus pertuzumab, supporting its recent US Food and Drug Administration approval and prompting questions regarding the necessity of chemotherapy, optimal duration of antibody-drug conjugate therapy, and the role of a dual ERBB2 blockade. Maintenance strategies have also expanded, particularly in hormone receptor–positive disease, with incorporation of endocrine therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitors, as demonstrated in the PATINA trial (NCT02947685). The HER2CLIMB-05 trial (NCT05132582) provided an additional maintenance approach using a triplet anti- ERBB2 strategy. These nonchemotherapy maintenance options are designed to have fewer toxic effects and better quality of life than chemotherapy-based strategies. These developments raise questions regarding the necessity of chemotherapy, optimal duration of antibody-drug conjugate therapy, and the role of dual ERBB2 blockade. Emerging biomarker-driven approaches, including the HER2DX assay and circulating tumor DNA, remain investigational and are not yet part of routine clinical practice but aim to optimize treatment selection. Novel strategies, such as chemotherapy-free regimens and sequential multiagent approaches, as in the SAPPHO study (NCT06439693), are challenging traditional paradigms. Conclusions and Relevance The management of ERBB2 -positive metastatic breast cancer is transitioning toward a more individualized approach that balances efficacy, toxic effects, and patient preferences. Integrating biomarker-driven strategies will be essential to optimize treatment selection, duration, and sequencing, with the goal of improving long-term outcomes while preserving quality of life.

proposals.title: Feasibility and Tolerability of Chemoimmunotherapy Given During Induction for Treatment of Patients With High-Risk Neuroblastoma: A Report From the Children's Oncology Group
proposals.abstract: Purpose The addition of the anti-GD2 antibody dinutuximab (DIN) to postconsolidation therapy led to improved event-free survival (EFS) for patients with high-risk neuroblastoma (HRNBL). The combination of DIN with chemotherapy (chemoimmunotherapy) results in objective responses in patients with recurrent/refractory neuroblastoma. We evaluated the feasibility of administering chemoimmunotherapy during induction for HRNBL in a multicenter trial. Methods Children's Oncology Group (COG) ANBL17P1 was a prospective, single-arm, limited institution pilot study to assess tolerability and feasibility of administering DIN and sargramostim with induction chemotherapy cycles 3-5. The primary end point of tolerability was assessed as the occurrence of a predefined unacceptable toxicity or toxic death during DIN-containing cycles. Feasibility was assessed as ability to receive ≥75% of planned DIN doses. Revised International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria were used to assess response. Results Forty eligible, evaluable patients with newly diagnosed HRNBL were enrolled at eight sites from January 2019 to June 2020. The most common DIN-related grade ≥3 toxicities during induction cycles 3-5 included fever (30.0%) and pain (7.5%). There were no unacceptable toxicities or toxic deaths during induction cycles 3-5. Patients received 92.0%-101.8% of intended induction DIN doses. This regimen was therefore deemed both feasible and tolerable. Thirty-seven patients completed all end-of-induction evaluations; 13 had complete response (CR), 22 partial response (PR), one minor response (MR), zero stable disease, and one progressive disease. The overall end of induction CR + PR rate was 87.5%. The 3-year EFS was 52.5% ± 7.9%. Conclusion Administration of DIN with COG induction cycles 3-5 for patients with newly diagnosed HRNBL was tolerable and feasible. This approach is currently being evaluated in a COG randomized phase III trial.

draft.name: Feasibility and Tolerability of Chemoimmunotherapy Given During Induction for Treatment of Patients With High-Risk Neuroblastoma: A Report From the Children's Oncology Group

proposals.title: Identifying novel genomic alterations in relapsed childhood B-ALL: a report from the Children's Oncology Group
proposals.abstract: Relapsed B-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) generally occurs due to the emergence of subclones resistant to therapy, leading to poor outcome. Here, we describe novel genomic alterations responsible for therapeutic resistance at a subtype level in a clinical trial (AALL1331) which randomized patients to blinatumomab and chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone. We performed whole-genome and transcriptome sequencing on 288 patients (183 diagnosis/first relapse/germline trios and 105 additional patients with first-relapse samples) and analyzed 41 second-relapse samples. For ETV6::RUNX1, we showed that cases with gain of the fusion allele or with fusion transcript involving exon 5 of ETV6 and exon 4 of RUNX1 (E5-E4) had a higher risk of first relapse than cases with E5-E3. For the hyperdiploid subtype, we demonstrated that low modal chromosomal numbers (51-52) were more prone to first relapse than those with ≥53 chromosomes, with an additive effect of CREBBP mutations. We showed enrichment of IKZF1 alterations in the Philadelphia-like subtype and that NSD2 E1099K was commonly associated with relapse in TCF3::PBX1. Together, these new features accounted for 30% (n=55) of first relapses. Intriguingly, ~3% of relapses are related to secondary B-ALL or germline predisposition. We also compared genomic alterations at diagnosis and first relapse in relation to second relapse status in randomized patients, with TCF3::PBX1/NT5C2 linked to worse outcomes regardless of randomized arm. Together, our findings provide novel insights into the genomics of relapsed childhood B-ALL as well as in the context of blinatumomab therapy. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as # NCT0201853.

proposals.title: Immunochemotherapy for Borderline Resectable or Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer: A Randomized Controlled Trial
proposals.abstract: Purpose The optimal treatment strategy for patients with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer (BRPC) and locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC) remains undefined. We evaluated whether the addition of programmed cell death protein 1 blockade to modified FOLFIRINOX improves outcomes compared with modified FOLFIRINOX alone. Methods In this open-label, randomized phase II trial, patients with histologically confirmed BRPC or LAPC were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive modified FOLFIRINOX plus toripalimab (immunochemotherapy) or modified FOLFIRINOX alone (chemotherapy). Treatment response was assessed every 2 months, and surgical eligibility was determined by a multidisciplinary team. The primary end point was event-free survival (EFS) in the intention-to-treat population. Results Between April 2019 and March 2025, 392 patients were randomly assigned to immunochemotherapy (n = 196) or chemotherapy (n = 196). After a median follow-up of 39.6 months, immunochemotherapy significantly improved EFS compared with chemotherapy (median, 11.1 v 9.6 months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.74 [95% CI, 0.60 to 0.92]; P =.007). The median overall survival (OS) was 20.6 versus 17.1 months (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.63 to 1.03). Objective response rates were 30.1% (59/196) and 18.9% (37/196), respectively. Tumor resection rates were 42.3% (83/196) and 43.9% (86/196), and R0 resection rates were 84.1% (69/82) and 74.7% (62/83), respectively. Prespecified subgroup analyses suggested improved EFS and OS in BRPC but not LAPC. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 47.9% (93/194) and 49.2% (96/195) of patients receiving immunochemotherapy and chemotherapy, respectively. Grade III or higher postoperative complications occurred in 30.1% (25/83) and 25.6% (22/86) of resected patients. Conclusion The addition of PD-1 blockade to modified FOLFIRINOX significantly improved EFS without increasing treatment-related toxicity or surgical morbidity in patients with BRPC or LAPC.

draft.name: Immunochemotherapy for Borderline Resectable or Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer: A Randomized Controlled Trial

proposals.title: Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy Versus Surgical Resection for Early-Stage Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer: An Emulated Target Trial
proposals.abstract: Purpose Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) is standard of care for inoperable early-stage non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but there is little evidence to support SABR as an alternative to surgical resection. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have failed to recruit, and ongoing RCTs apply strict inclusion criteria. To our knowledge, this is the first emulated target trial comparing the effectiveness of SABR versus surgery in individuals with early-stage NSCLC eligible for either treatment. Methods We used England's National Cancer Registry data to identify individuals diagnosed with T1-2N0M0 NSCLC during 2015-2020, age 18-79 years with Zubrod performance status 0-2, or age 80+ years with performance status 0-1, who underwent SABR or surgical resection within 6 months of diagnosis. Treatment receipt was identified via linkage to Hospital Episode Statistics and the National Radiotherapy Data Set. The primary outcome was 3-year all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes included lung cancer–specific mortality and recurrence. An instrumental variable analysis reduced the risk of confounding by indication. Results A total of 12,546 met the eligibility criteria (2,299 SABR; 10,247 surgery). After adjustment, 3-year all-cause mortality estimates were 30.3% (SABR) and 21.6% (surgery; mean absolute risk difference 8.8 percentage points [pp], [95% CI, 1.4 to 16.2]; P =.02). Lung cancer–specific mortality estimates were 20.6% (SABR) and 14.5% (surgery; mean absolute risk difference 6.1 pp [95% CI, –0.6 to 12.9]; P =.07). The adjusted mean absolute risk difference in 3-year all-cause mortality for those age 80+ years was 4.3 pp ([95% CI, –3.7 to 12.3]; P =.62). Conclusion This emulated target trial found higher 3-year all-cause mortality after SABR versus surgery in early-stage NSCLC suitable for either modality, supporting that surgical resection should remain the preferred option. The findings support SABR as a curative-intent alternative, particularly for older people.

draft.name: Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy Versus Surgical Resection for Early-Stage Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer: An Emulated Target Trial

proposals.title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
proposals.abstract: Ribosomal frameshifting, an uncommon translational recoding event, is best known for its regulatory roles in viral gene expression1,2, whereas its physiological relevance in mammals remains poorly understood. Here we show that specific codon pairs trigger efficient -1 frameshifting preferentially in cancer cells. Mechanistically, this recoding arises from ribosomal pausing associated with tRNA and amino acid availability, and is amplified by impaired ribosome quality control and sustained phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6. We found that this codon-pair-specific frameshifting represents an intrinsic state of translational dysregulation, which is prevalent across cancer cells and reshapes protein synthesis. Taking advantage of this frameshifting-permissive state in cancer cells, we engineered a frameshifting-activated synthetic therapeutic circuit (FAST) that conditionally expresses the pyroptotic effector gasdermin D. FAST is activated across diverse cancer cell types, inducing potent and selective pyroptosis, while sparing normal tissues from detectable toxicity. As a proof of concept, systemic AAV9-mediated delivery of FAST in mouse models of colorectal and pancreatic cancer elicited pronounced tumour regression, robust immune activation and synergistic effects with immune checkpoint blockade. Collectively, these findings reveal codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting as a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells and establish translation-coupled gene circuits as a strategy for cancer-selective therapy.

proposals.title: Circulating Tumor DNA Profiling Across Phase II/III Ewing Sarcoma Trials Identifies High-Risk Patients With TP53 , STAG2 , and CDKN2A Alterations
proposals.abstract: PURPOSE Ewing sarcoma is an aggressive bone cancer driven by FET::ETS fusions, with few recurrent secondary genomic alterations (most commonly involving STAG2, TP53, and CDKN2A) and copy-number variants. Currently, diagnosis relies exclusively on tumor biopsies and imaging, and despite a well-defined genomic landscape, risk stratification remains based solely on clinicoradiologic parameters. Furthermore, tumor evolution and intrapatient heterogeneity remain poorly characterized, and prospective evidence supporting molecular risk stratification is limited. MATERIALS AND METHODS We prospectively integrated serial circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) sampling into the first-line phase II/III Euro Ewing 2012 (EE2012) and CombinaiR3 trials, complemented by relapse studies. Across 347 patients, 991 blood, tumor, and bone marrow samples were profiled using custom targeted sequencing and shallow whole-genome sequencing to enable integrated biologic characterization and clinical correlative analyses. RESULTS ctDNA recapitulated established Ewing sarcoma genomic landscapes while also revealing intrapatient tumor heterogeneity when compared with matched tumor biopsy profiles. Blood and bone marrow plasma profiles were highly concordant. Longitudinal sampling identified selection of TP53 -altered clones at relapse. Clinically, detection of TP53 and/or STAG2 loss-of-function mutations and/or CDKN2A focal deletions in ctDNA at diagnosis predicted poor outcomes and, in a multivariable model adjusting for metastatic status, tumor volume, age, and treatment, defined an independent molecular high-risk subgroup with inferior event-free survival (hazard ratio [HR], 3.6 [95% CI, 2.2 to 5.8], P <.001) and overall survival (HR, 4.3 [95% CI, 2.5 to 7.3], P <.001) in EE2012 patients. CONCLUSION Prospective, trial-integrated ctDNA profiling provides comprehensive molecular characterization, reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity and clonal evolution, and identifies an independent molecular high-risk subgroup at diagnosis, supporting ctDNA-guided risk stratification in Ewing sarcoma.

draft.name: Circulating Tumor DNA Profiling Across Phase II/III Ewing Sarcoma Trials Identifies High-Risk Patients With TP53 , STAG2 , and CDKN2A Alterations
draft.authors: Mous L, Ballet S, Dureau S, et al.

proposals.title: Longitudinal remodeling of the tumor-immune microenvironment during regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer
proposals.abstract: Previous studies combining the multikinase inhibitor regorafenib with a PD-1 inhibitor showed promising activity in gastric cancer. We conducted a phase 1b/2 trial (NCT05394740) of first-line regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in 30 patients with mismatch repair–proficient gastric cancer and investigated its impact on the tumor microenvironment. The primary end point was met; 22 of 30 patients showed objective tumor response (73%; 80% confidence interval, 60.3 to 83.8). Single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing were performed on biopsy samples at baseline, during treatment, and at disease progression. The combination treatment increased tumor antigen–reactive CD8+ T cells and M1-like proinflammatory macrophages and decreased immunosuppressive and tumor-promoting populations, including activated CCR8+ regulatory T cells, LRRC15+ cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), RGS5+ pericytes, and APLN+ tip cells. At progression, LRRC15+ CAFs and APLN+ tip cells remained reduced, activated CCR8+ regulatory T cells reexpanded, and additional treatment-resistant subsets emerged, including APOC1+ lipid-associated macrophages. In murine models of acquired resistance, therapeutic targeting of these suppressive immune cell populations with antibodies against CCR8 or TREM2 in combination with PD-1 blockade restored antitumor immunity. These findings demonstrate dynamic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

draft.name: Longitudinal remodeling of the tumor-immune microenvironment during regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer
draft.authors: Itahashi K, Kawazoe A, Hashimoto T, et al.

proposals.title: Retinoblastoma
proposals.abstract: Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, represents a substantial global health equity concern, exemplifying profound disparities in global burden and outcome despite being a largely curable cancer. Retinoblastoma is thought to arise from cone photoreceptor precursor cells of the developing retina, mainly driven by biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene. Fewer than 2% of cases have no detectable RB1 pathogenic variant; approximately half of these cases instead show high-level amplification of the MYCN oncogene. Diagnosis and monitoring currently rely on clinical examination and multimodal imaging. Emerging molecular diagnostic approaches such as aqueous humour liquid biopsy hold promise for minimally invasive tumour characterisation and real-time disease monitoring. Management has shifted towards eye-preserving strategies, with intra-arterial, intravitreal, and intracameral chemotherapy showing efficacy and safety. The global burden and mortality of retinoblastoma remains highest in regions with a low sociodemographic index, highlighting the need for continued interdisciplinary, equity-focused efforts to ensure timely diagnosis and accessible, high-quality care worldwide. This Seminar reviews the advances in retinoblastoma biology, diagnosis, treatment, survivorship, and global efforts to reduce inequities.

proposals.title: Estimated global treatment costs for 31 cancer types by stage, year, and follow-up period: a systematic review and modelling study
proposals.abstract: Background Cancer is a growing health and economic burden worldwide, yet comprehensive global estimates of cancer treatment costs are sparse. Such data are crucial for economic evaluations to inform policy making and practice to improve cancer control and outcomes. We aimed to synthesise available estimates of direct cancer treatment costs by stage, year, and follow-up period and predict global cancer treatment costs. Methods In this systematic review and modelling study, we extracted estimates of cancer treatment costs (ie, direct treatment costs only) from the medical literature, screening 25 896 studies, of which 196 were included in our final dataset, covering 31 cancer types across 44 countries. Costs were standardised as a ratio of country GDP per capita and adjusted for follow-up period. We used a Bayesian hierarchical model to synthesise the estimates as a function of GDP per capita, accounting for cancer type, stage (I-IV), year of diagnosis, and follow-up period. We then estimated global and regional treatment costs (overall and by cancer type) in US$ 2022 based on the latest available incidence data from GLOBOCAN. This study is registered on PROSPERO (#CRD420251138446). Findings Globally, total 10-year treatment costs for newly diagnosed cancers in 2022 were estimated to be $771·48 billion (95% UI 719·99-823·81), with breast cancer being the largest driver of costs ($96·07 billion [80·78-109·43]), followed by leukaemia ($86·11 billion [80·36-94·87]) and lung cancer ($84·36 billion [73·18-95·28]). North America and Europe accounted for 64% of total costs, but only 36% of diagnosed cancer cases. Mean costs per diagnosed patient were $38 650 (95% UI 36 070-41 280) globally, ranging from $3380 (95% UI 2960-3820) in eastern Africa to $93 600 (95% UI 87 170-100 150) in North America. As a ratio of GDP per capita, treatment costs declined with increasing GDP per capita (from 3·16 [95% UI 2·61-3·81] at $500 GDP per capita to 1·36 [1·07-1·70] at $100 000 GDP per capita), especially for stage IV cancers, which declined from 8·06 (6·57-9·61) at $500 GDP per capita to 4·53 (3·48-5·83) at $100 000 GDP per capita. Cancer types with the highest mean cost ratios were bone cancer (6·27 [95% UI 2·45-11·73]), leukaemia (6·16 [5·59-7·01]), and multiple myeloma (5·74 [3·78-6·74]). Treatment costs remained stable over time by year of diagnosis for stage I-II cancers, but steadily increased for stage III cancers, and rose substantially for stage IV cancers. Interpretation These cost estimates provide new important data for economic evaluations, which can support expenditure planning, priority setting, and policy making to help guide strategic investment and resource allocations to improve cancer care and outcomes across different settings. Funding Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

proposals.title: Expanding the RAS-verse: Novel Inhibitors, Emergent Dependencies, Fresh Opportunities in RAS -Mutant NSCLC
proposals.abstract: Summary: In this issue, two studies establish KRASG13C as a directly targetable oncoprotein in non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) while revealing distinct dependence of codon 13–mutant NSCLC on wild-type (WT) RAS and enhanced sensitivity to standard-of-care chemotherapy. A third study highlights rewired oncogenic signaling through WT RAS as a therapeutically tractable mechanism of resistance to KRASG12C inhibitors in the context of acquired oncogenic kinase fusions. proposals.title: Image-Based Consensus Molecular Subtyping Refines Prognostication in Stage II/III Colorectal Cancer: A Retrospective Analysis of the SCOT Trial
proposals.abstract: Purpose Risk stratification in localized colorectal cancer (CRC) remains inadequate. Transcriptome-based classifiers such as consensus molecular subtyping (CMS) improve this, but are challenging to implement. We determined the performance of a novel image-based method for CRC CMS subtyping (imCMS) using routine pathology images from the SCOT trial and investigated association of imCMS subtypes with clinicopathologic and tumor molecular and immune factors, treatment benefit, and survival. Methods We applied a novel imCMS classifier to stage II/III CRCs from the SCOT trial (ISRCTN59757862) which examined 3 versus 6 months of adjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy following curative-intent surgery. We determined correlates of imCMS subgroups and investigated imCMS prognostic and predictive value for CRC recurrence-free interval, overall survival (OS), and survival after CRC recurrence (SAR) by univariable and multivariable Cox regression. Results A total of 2,816 cases were informative for imCMS classification, of which 664 (24%) were imCMS1 (immune), 987 (35%) imCMS2 (canonical), 433 (15%) imCMS3 (metabolic), 653 (23%) imCMS4 (mesenchymal), and 79 (3%) of mixed subtype. Analysis confirmed expected associations of imCMS1 with deficient DNA mismatch repair (dMMR) and imCMS3 with KRAS mutation and revealed substantially lower intraepithelial CD8+ and intrastromal FoxP3+ T-cell infiltrate (CD8IE -FoxP3IS) in imCMS4 tumors. imCMS classification was strongly prognostic independent of clinicopathologic factors, dMMR, and CD8IE -FoxP3IS in multivariable analysis but did not predict differential benefit from chemotherapy duration or regimen. The combination of imCMS with CD8IE -FoxP3IS groups defined CRC subgroups with substantially different recurrence risk. Analysis of OS and SAR revealed notable discordance in imCMS3 and imCMS4 prognostic value before and after relapse. Conclusion imCMS classification improves CRC prognostication beyond existing tumor factors and is potentially deliverable in clinical practice. imCMS prediction of therapeutic benefit requires further study.

draft.name: Image-Based Consensus Molecular Subtyping Refines Prognostication in Stage II/III Colorectal Cancer: A Retrospective Analysis of the SCOT Trial

proposals.title: The Transformation of Oncology Drug Development in China: Toward a New Phase of Innovation
proposals.abstract: China’s oncology drug development ecosystem has shifted from rapid pipeline expansion toward clinical value–driven innovation. We review regulatory reform and the 2015 to 2025 evolution of clinical development across small molecules, mAbs, multispecific antibodies, antibody–drug conjugates, and cell and gene therapies. China’s disease burden and enrollment capacity have enabled globally relevant advances in EGFR-mutant lung cancer, gastrointestinal malignancies, hepatocellular carcinoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and CLDN18.2-directed therapies. We highlight persistent challenges in target and modality convergence, biomarker definition, therapeutic window optimization, manufacturing consistency, and globally interpretable evidence generation and discuss how artificial intelligence may connect target discovery, drug design, and clinical trial optimization more efficiently. Significance: China has become a major source of oncology trials and modality innovation, but scale alone will not ensure global impact. This review links regulatory reform, disease-specific opportunity, target biology, therapeutic format, and evidence quality across a decade of solid tumor development. It defines the conditions under which China-originated programs can generate globally practice-changing evidence. See related article by Shi, p. XX.

proposals.title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
proposals.abstract: Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour. However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.

draft.name: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
draft.authors: de Jong G, Memi F, Gracia T, et al.

proposals.title: Autophagy-mediated Secretion of Intracellular Antigens Co-opts Antibody Responses to Drive Neutrophil-Dependent Tumor Progression
proposals.abstract: How intracellular proteins, normally hidden from the immune system, become targets of tumor-associated antibody responses remains unresolved, as does the function of such autoantibodies encoded by tumor-infiltrating B cells (TIL-Bs). Using monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) cloned from TIL-Bs in a spontaneous hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) model, we define a class of antigens: secreted intracellular antigens (SICAs). Tumors co-opt upregulated autophagy to release cytosolic proteins, exemplified by ALDH1L1, through HSP90-mediated autophagy-dependent unconventional secretion. The resulting autoantibodies form immune complexes at the tumor site, where the SICA is locally available, recruiting and reprogramming neutrophils into tumor-associated neutrophils that drive tumor progression. Both neutrophil depletion and loss of Fcγ receptor binding abolish this effect. Autophagy-mediated SICA secretion and the corresponding autoantibody response are conserved in HCC patients and extend to lung, breast and cervical cancers. Tumors thus reshape their secretome to hijack humoral immunity, highlighting the SICA–autoantibody–FcγR axis as a potential therapeutic target.

draft.name: Autophagy-mediated Secretion of Intracellular Antigens Co-opts Antibody Responses to Drive Neutrophil-Dependent Tumor Progression

proposals.title: Cancer in the Commonwealth: a Lancet Oncology Commission
proposals.abstract: Cancer is now one of the defining health and development challenges of our time. The 56 nations of the Commonwealth, home to 2·7 billion people, mirror this global burden. Recorded cancer cases across member states rose by 35% in 2008-18 and the number of deaths reached almost 1·7 million in 2018. The Lancet Oncology Commission on cancer in the Commonwealth was convened to ask a deceptively simple question: how can 56 diverse nations act collectively to close the widening gap between the burden of cancer and the capacity of each country to respond? 80 researchers, clinicians, policy makers, and civil society members, organised into five working groups and ten research streams, spent 2 years assembling the evidence base for this report. Using a validated microsimulation model, we estimate that 5-year net survival across eleven common cancers in the Commonwealth stood at just 30·7% in 2020, ranging from 4·1% in low-income countries (LICs) to 59·0% in high-income countries (HICs), driven overwhelmingly by late-stage presentation, which affects 62% of patients in LICs compared with 43% in HICs. This difference in survival is compounded by chronic underinvestment. Infrastructure gaps are equally stark: only 12% of countries meet international benchmarks for CT imaging, 22% for hospital density, and 40% for radiotherapy. Governance is underdeveloped too: barely one-third of Commonwealth countries have a national cancer control plan meeting basic quality criteria. Research investment also mirrors these inequities: between 2016 and 2023, Commonwealth countries collectively invested only US$165 per cancer-related disability adjusted life year. Yet the case for investment is unambiguous. Our modelling shows that a comprehensive scaleup of treatment, imaging, and quality of care could raise 5-year net survival across the Commonwealth from 30·7% to 52·9%, averting an estimated 5·8 million deaths and adding 113 million life-years between 2025 and 2035, at an incremental cost of $36·7 billion, delivering a return of between four and twenty dollars on every dollar invested. Crucially, this investment need not depend chiefly on external aid, which is contracting sharply at present. Our modelling for 38 low-income and middle-income Commonwealth countries suggests that up to $701 billion in additional domestic fiscal space could be mobilised between 2025 and 2030, through budget reprioritisation, macroeconomic growth, targeted taxation, and prudent borrowing. On this evidence, the Commission proposes six priority actions. These commitments are ambitious, set against an unusually turbulent geopolitical backdrop of declining official development assistance, fiscal retrenchment, and contested multilateralism. Yet it is precisely this backdrop that gives the Commonwealth its distinctive advantage: a voluntary association spanning every income level and continent, bound by common legal and regulatory traditions, capable of collective action that neither purely bilateral aid nor multilateral institutions under strain can easily replicate.

draft.name: Cancer in the Commonwealth: a Lancet Oncology Commission
draft.authors: Atun R, Sirohi B, Jaffray D, et al.

proposals.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
proposals.abstract: Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

draft.name: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
draft.authors: Saraswat M, Rueda-Gensini L, Heinzelmann E, et al.

proposals.title: Spatiotemporal control of CAR-T cell TNF release via tumor-targeted irradiation
proposals.abstract: Adoptive chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies have limited efficacy in solid tumors because of poor infiltration and impaired effector function, whereas radiotherapy is constrained by radioresistance and metastatic spread. Here we show that integrating the spatial precision of ionizing radiation with the biological specificity of CAR-T cells enables localized delivery of the inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF). We identified radiation-responsive genes in tumor-infiltrating T cells and engineered synthetic radioinducible promoters to drive TNF expression. Human CAR-T cells carrying this construct (riTNF CAR-T cells) secreted high levels of TNF upon irradiation, independently of antigen engagement. In human xenograft and murine tumor models, the combination of riTNF CAR-T cells and local irradiation produced greater tumor regression than either treatment alone or standard CAR-T cells with irradiation. This response was associated with high intratumoral, but not systemic, TNF levels, increased tumor necrosis and apoptosis, vascular disruption and greater CAR-T cell infiltration. These findings establish a platform for spatially and temporally controlled cytokine delivery from engineered CAR-T cells.

draft.name: Spatiotemporal control of CAR-T cell TNF release via tumor-targeted irradiation
draft.authors: Masoumi E, Walczak P, Tsuji T, et al.

proposals.title: Global Proposal for the TNM Staging System for Poorly Differentiated Thyroid Cancer
proposals.abstract: Importance Poorly differentiated thyroid cancer (PDTC) lacks a dedicated staging system, requiring use of the eighth version of the American Joint Committee on Cancer and Union for International Cancer Control TNM staging system (TNM-8) for differentiated thyroid cancer despite its distinct biology. Objective To develop a PDTC-specific staging system. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study analyzed data from the International Aggressive Thyroid Cancer Collaborative Group (IATCCG), including surgically treated patients at 91 centers in 14 countries from January 1984 to January 2026. External validation was performed using patients from the US Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database. Data were analyzed from December 2025 to June 2026. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary end point was overall survival. With M1 disease predefined as stage IVB, the schema for stages I–IVA in patients with M0 disease were redefined. All possible TN combinations were fitted into multivariable Cox models, with the lowest Akaike information criterion defining the proposed system. Prognostic discrimination was assessed using adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) and C statistics. Results Among 1010 patients in the IATCCG cohort, 610 (60.4%) were female, and the median (IQR) age at diagnosis was 58 (46-68) years; median (IQR) follow-up was 41 (15-85) months. Among 170 patients in the SEER cohort, 85 (50.0%) were female, and the median (IQR) age at diagnosis was 61 (49-72) years; median (IQR) follow-up was 92 (42-154) months. In the IATCCG cohort, level VII lymph node metastasis (LNM) was associated with lower 5-year overall survival (45.2%; 95% CI, 33.4-61.2) than level VI (73.2%; 95% CI, 64.4-83.3) or lateral neck LNM (56.7%; 95% CI, 49.4-65.0). Level VII LNM was therefore reclassified from N1a to N1c. The lowest Akaike information criterion configuration among 16 738 candidates defined stages I to IVA as follows: I, T1N0/NX/N1a or T2N0/NX; II, T1N1b/N1c, T2N1a/N1b, or T3N0/NX/N1a; III, T2N1c, T3N1b, or T4aN0/NX/N1a; IVA, T3N1c, T4aN1b/N1c, or T4b any N; and IVB, M1 disease. Compared with TNM-8, stage I disease decreased from 44.4% (448 of 1010) to 24.6% (248 of 1010) and stage IV disease increased from 18.5% (187 of 1010) to 32.4% (327 of 1010) with the proposed system. The proposed staging had a higher C statistic than TNM-8 (0.74 [95% CI, 0.71-0.76] vs 0.71 [95% CI, 0.68-0.74]; difference, 0.03; 95% CI, 0.01-0.04). Corresponding SEER C statistic values were 0.76 (95% CI, 0.71-0.81) vs 0.74 (95% CI, 0.68-0.79), respectively (difference, 0.02; 95% CI, −0.01 to 0.06). Conclusions and Relevance This cohort study found that this PDTC-specific staging system provides improved prognostic stratification reflecting its different biology. These data provide a strong rationale for the potential inclusion of a stand-alone American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system for PDTC.

draft.name: Global Proposal for the TNM Staging System for Poorly Differentiated Thyroid Cancer
draft.authors: Shi X, Liu Q, Scholfield D, et al.

proposals.title: Longitudinal single-cell profiling of breast tumors highlights immune and epigenetic mechanisms associated with sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors
proposals.abstract: Estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer treatment is based primarily on endocrine therapy. To dissect mechanisms of sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors in ER-positive breast cancer, we profiled tumor biopsies from 25 patients during neoadjuvant therapy using single-cell RNA sequencing, immune receptor sequencing and enhancer activity mapping. Malignant cells with high ER signaling and elevated activity of enhancers with ER binding sites were sensitive to treatment. Resistance was associated with androgen receptor signaling, dedifferentiation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Poor responders preferentially used the androgen receptor cis-regulome under treatment pressure. The baseline tumor microenvironment was associated with tumor downstaging. Poor responders exhibited a 'hot', yet ineffective immune landscape enriched for naive lymphoid and undifferentiated myeloid cells. Good responders showed an active immune microenvironment with sustained clonal expansion of T cells. Our longitudinal single-cell analyses elucidate the genetic, cellular and epigenetic mechanisms driving sensitivity and resistance to neoadjuvant aromatase inhibition in ER-positive breast cancer.

draft.name: Longitudinal single-cell profiling of breast tumors highlights immune and epigenetic mechanisms associated with sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors
draft.authors: Altinönder I, Winton V, Quý KL, et al.

proposals.title: Myeloid-derived TGFβ1 and oncostatin M establish two distinct stromal niches controlling late and hybrid EMT states
proposals.abstract: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) regulates tumor progression, metastasis and resistance to therapy. EMT encompasses a continuum of tumor states displaying different functions. The precise dialog between the tumor microenvironment and the different EMT states remains poorly understood. Using single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of mouse skin tumors, we uncover that different EMT states are associated with different niches. Neutrophils are more abundant in niches associated with hybrid EMT and secreted oncostatin M, which partially activates EMT while sustaining the epithelial program, promoting hybrid EMT states and metastasis formation. Macrophages are more abundant in niches associated with more advanced EMT states, which, together with other stromal cells, express TGFβ1 that promotes the late EMT state. Oncostatin M and TGFβ1 function in a feed-forward manner by creating distinct inflammatory niches to maintain specific EMT states. Together, our results reveal that distinct niches are associated with specific EMT states and that signaling pathways sustain their own niche's identity by recruiting specific myeloid cell populations.

draft.name: Myeloid-derived TGFβ1 and oncostatin M establish two distinct stromal niches controlling late and hybrid EMT states
draft.authors: Dong A, Vanuytven S, González AP, et al.

proposals.title: Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substance Exposure and Breast Cancer Incidence in the Sister Study
proposals.abstract: Purpose Although mechanistic evidence suggests that some per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) may be carcinogenic, epidemiologic findings for PFAS and breast cancer remain inconsistent, partly because of differing study designs and limited evaluation by hormone receptor status. Methods We conducted a case-cohort study within the Sister Study that included 1,609 breast cancer cases and 2,269 subcohort participants. We oversampled estrogen receptor (ER)–negative cases (324 ER-negative, 1,120 ER-positive) to improve statistical power. Seventeen PFASs were quantified in prediagnostic plasma using liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry. Sampling-weighted Cox models were used to estimate associations with overall breast cancer incidence and by hormone receptor status, adjusting for confounders and coexposures. We conducted a meta-analysis of seven studies with prediagnostic blood PFAS measurements. Results We observed associations between certain PFAS and ER-negative tumors. Positive associations were observed for perfluoro-n-octanoic acid (PFOA; hazard ratio [HR] Q4 v Q1, 1.67 [95% CI, 1.10 to 2.53], P trend =.09), perfluorooctane-1-sulfonic acid (PFOS; HR Q4 v Q1, 1.93 [95% CI, 1.15 to 3.22], P trend =.01), and potentially n-methylperfluoro-1-octanesulfonamidoacetic acid (N-MeFOSAA; HR Q4 v Q1, 1.42 [95% CI, 0.99 to 2.04], P trend =.12). By contrast, perfluoro-n-tridecanoic acid was inversely associated with ER-negative tumors (PFTrDA; HR Q4 v Q1, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.41 to 0.97], P trend =.05). Perfluorooctane sulfonamide (PFOSA), which was infrequently detected (6.9%), was positively associated with ER+ tumors (HR detectable v nondetectable, 1.36 [95% CI, 1.03 to 1.81]). The meta-analysis further supported associations for both PFOA (relative risk [RR], 1.30 [95% CI, 1.05 to 1.62]) and PFOS with ER-negative breast cancer (RR, 1.20 [95% CI, 0.91 to 1.58]). Conclusion Findings from this large prospective study, together with meta-analyses, suggest that PFOA and PFOS may increase ER-negative breast cancer risk. Given the widespread exposure to PFAS and limited established risk factors for ER-negative tumors, these results have important public health implications.

draft.name: Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substance Exposure and Breast Cancer Incidence in the Sister Study
draft.authors: Chang C, Pullella K, Keil AP, et al.

proposals.title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression
proposals.abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1+) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8+ T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.

draft.authors: Pan Q, Wang X, Li Y, et al.

proposals.title: International Initiative on a Refined Staging System for Medullary Thyroid Cancer: A Multinational Multicenter Study
proposals.abstract: PURPOSE To refine the suboptimal prognostic discrimination of the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition TNM (TNM-8) staging system for medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). METHODS This retrospective study enrolled patients with MTC from 43 centers across 15 countries under the framework of the International Medullary Thyroid Cancer Staging Consortium (IMTCSC). Pooled data were analyzed with disease-specific survival as the primary end point. With M1 disease fixed in stage IVC, we redefined the schema for stages I to IVB in M0 patients. Using exhaustive enumeration, all possible TN combinations were fitted into multivariable Cox models, with the lowest Akaike information criterion (AIC) defining the proposed system. Prognostic discrimination was assessed using adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) and the concordance index (C-index). RESULTS The IMTCSC cohort included 2,573 patients with MTC (female-to-male ratio: 1.25; median age 52 years [IQR, 41-62]; median follow-up 76.3 months [IQR, 37.3-121.0]). Level VII metastasis correlated with poorer survival, supporting its upgrade to N1c. Exhaustive search of 116,284 admissible stage-grouping schemas identified the optimal model (lowest AIC) defining stages I to IVB: I (T1N0-N1a/T2N0), II (T1N1b/T2N1a/T3N0), III (T1N1c/T2N1b/T3N1a/T4aN0-N1a), IVA (T2N1c/T3N1b-N1c/T4aN1b), and IVB (T4aN1c/T4b any N). Compared with AJCC TNM-8 (stage I as reference; stage II aHR, 0.84, P =.652; stage III aHR, 1.48, P =.172; stage IV aHR, 7.95, P <.001), the proposed system showed a clearer monotonic increase in disease-specific death risk (stage II aHR 2.22; stage III aHR, 4.81; stage IV aHR 15.75; all P ≤.001) and a higher C-index (0.892 v 0.856, P <.001), which was also evaluated in the SEER cohort (N = 1,909). CONCLUSION The proposed MTC staging system confers an improved schema for prognostic stratification compared with AJCC TNM-8.

proposals.title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
proposals.abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.
